title: How to open, scope and drive a design round
story:
An open-ended design question has no correct answer, and the failure is almost never ignorance of a component. It is answering a question nobody asked, at a level of detail nobody wanted, having never established what the thing has to do.

So the first move is not a diagram. Spend the opening minutes establishing three things: the scale, the shape of the traffic, and what must not fail. Scale decides everything downstream — a design for a thousand users and a design for a hundred million share no decisions. Traffic shape decides more than volume does: read-heavy and write-heavy are different systems, and steady and bursty are different systems again. And what must not fail is the question that separates a design that loses a like from one that loses a payment, which is the difference between eventual consistency being fine and being unacceptable.

Then state the simplest design that meets what you established, and say it is the simplest design. One service, one database, synchronous calls. Two things happen when you do this. You have something concrete to attack, which is what the rest of the round is for. And you have demonstrated the judgement that the exercise is actually testing, because reaching for queues and sharding before establishing scale is the most common way to fail a design round while appearing knowledgeable.

Now break it deliberately, and the numbers are what let you do that rather than guess. A main memory reference is around a hundred nanoseconds, a datacenter round trip around five hundred thousand, a disk seek around ten million, a megabyte read sequentially from disk around thirty million — so you can say out loud whether a step is affordable at the stated scale. Items in the system equals arrival rate times time in system, independently of the arrival distribution, the service distribution and the service order, so you can check a capacity claim without knowing the workload's shape. And fan-out inherits the worst case rather than the average: with a single server at a ninety-ninth percentile of one second, a fan-out to a hundred servers sees a slow response more often than not, and at two thousand servers even a one in ten thousand chance means eighteen percent of requests exceed a second.

Repair what broke, one thing at a time, and say what each repair costs. That is the whole shape: establish, simplify, break, repair, price. The candidate who reaches the same architecture by that route is doing something different from the one who recited it, and the difference is visible.

problem.name: Driving a design conversation
problem.shape: An open-ended design question is asked, with the constraints deliberately unstated.
tell: a diagram is being drawn before scale was established
the design is elaborate and the traffic is unknown
nobody has asked what must not fail
problem.move: Establish scale, traffic shape and what must not fail before proposing anything. State the simplest design that meets them and label it as such. Then break it deliberately using numbers rather than intuition, repair one thing at a time, and price each repair.
problem.invariant: Every architectural decision is downstream of scale, traffic shape and failure tolerance, so a design proposed before those are known cannot be evaluated — by you or by anyone else.
problem.breaks: Establishing scope commits you to numbers early, and those numbers constrain everything afterwards. That is the point and it is uncomfortable, because a stated assumption can be challenged in a way an unstated one cannot — which is exactly why it is worth stating.

cost.time: the opening minutes spent not answering, which feel like not answering
cost.beats: proposing a known architecture immediately, which is faster and demonstrates recall rather than judgement, and asking endless questions, which never arrives at a design

worked.problem: How do you open when the question is deliberately vague?
worked.reasoning:
By refusing to design until three things are established, and being explicit that this is what you are doing rather than appearing to stall.

The three are scale, traffic shape and what must not fail.

Scale, because every decision downstream depends on it and nothing above it does. A thousand users and a hundred million users share no architectural decisions. If the number is not given, propose one and say you are proposing it — assume a hundred million users, ten thousand requests per second at peak — because a stated assumption can be corrected while an unstated one silently governs everything you say afterwards.

Traffic shape, because it decides more than volume. Read-heavy and write-heavy are different systems: one is a caching and replication problem, the other is a partitioning and durability problem. Steady and bursty are different again, one being a capacity question and the other a queueing question. Volume alone does not distinguish them.

And what must not fail, which is the question people skip and the one that determines the consistency model. Losing a like is a different system from losing a payment. That single distinction decides whether eventual consistency is fine or unacceptable, and it cannot be recovered later by adding components.

Then I would state the simplest design that meets those and label it as the simplest — one service, one database, synchronous calls. This does two things. It puts something concrete on the table to attack, which is what the remaining time is for. And it demonstrates the judgement being tested, because reaching for queues, sharding and event sourcing before establishing scale is the commonest way to fail while appearing knowledgeable.

Then break it deliberately, using numbers so it is analysis rather than performance. A datacenter round trip is around five hundred thousand nanoseconds and a disk seek around ten million, so I can say aloud whether a step is affordable at the stated scale. Items in the system equals arrival rate times time in system, independently of the distributions and the service order, so a capacity claim is checkable without knowing the workload. And fan-out inherits the worst case — at a ninety-ninth percentile of one second, fanning out to a hundred servers sees a slow response more often than not, and at two thousand even one in ten thousand leaves eighteen percent of requests over a second.

Repair one thing at a time and price each repair. Adding a cache costs invalidation. Adding a queue costs a result-delivery path. Adding replicas costs staleness. A design presented without costs is a design that has not been thought about.

The meta-point I would keep in mind throughout: the exercise is not testing whether I know the components. It is testing whether I can establish what is needed, choose deliberately, and say what each choice costs — and the route to the architecture is the thing being observed, not the architecture.

problem.practice: Take any system you use daily and open it as though asked cold: write the three establishing questions, propose numbers for each, state the simplest design, then name the first thing that breaks at ten times your assumed scale.

beats.broke: An open-ended design question has no correct answer, and the failure is almost never ignorance of a component — it is answering a question nobody asked, at a level of detail nobody wanted, having never established what the thing has to do.
beats.fix: Spend the first minutes establishing scale, traffic shape and what must not fail, then state the simplest design that meets it, then break it deliberately and repair what broke.
beats.cost: Establishing scope costs time that feels like not answering, and the numbers you commit to early constrain everything afterwards — which is the point, and is uncomfortable.

interview.q: How do you open when the question is deliberately vague?
interview.trap: Proposing an architecture immediately to demonstrate knowledge. That is the commonest way to fail while appearing knowledgeable — reaching for queues and sharding before scale is established shows recall rather than the judgement being tested.
